problem.title: Why LUMI Was Created
problem.paragraph1: Choosing renewable energy can be difficult. Information about costs, weather conditions, energy use, and available technologies is often spread across different sources and can be hard to understand. LUMI brings this information together in one place and explains it in a simpler way.

irena.reShareTooltip: RE Share is the percentage of the Philippines' total electricity that came from renewable sources like solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal in the most recent IRENA year. A higher value means a larger share of clean energy.
irena.whyItMattersContent: IRENA tracks the Philippines' national renewable energy progress across all technologies. Comparing capacity, generation, and share against DOE data helps show whether the country is on track to meet its clean-energy targets. For a household, this context explains why rooftop solar, small wind, or micro-hydro can contribute to a national shift toward more affordable and reliable power.

provincialDemand.title: Provincial Demand
provincialDemand.loading: Loading DOE Annex 8 regional consumption data...
provincialDemand.note: Electricity consumption by sector per region (GWh). Sourced from DOE Annex 8.

insight.title: What you are seeing
insight.description: This chart shows how much electricity each Philippine region used in 2025, broken down by who uses it: homes (green), businesses (blue), factories (orange), and government or street lighting (gray). NCR and Calabarzon (IV-A) tower over the rest because they are the country’s economic and population hubs — think of them as the “engine rooms” of the Philippines. Smaller bars do not mean those regions are less important; they simply have fewer people and industries connected to the main grid. Some remote or island regions may also rely more on local generators rather than the national grid, so their numbers here can look lower than their actual energy use.
insight.whyDescription: The Philippines has 17 administrative regions. The data here follows the Department of Energy’s 2025 reporting format, which still labels the Bangsamoro region as “ARMM” (its older name). The now-dissolved Negros Island Region (NIR) is excluded because it was re-merged into Western Visayas (VI) and Central Visayas (VII) in 2015.

consumption.title: Total Electricity Use Over Time
consumption.subtitle: How much electricity the whole country uses, and where it's heading

explanation.what: This chart shows historical national electricity consumption in the Philippines and the forecast through 2030.
explanation.why: Higher consumption means more power plants are needed. It also means more opportunities for clean energy to replace fossil fuels.
explanation.action: If your region shows above-average growth, consider solar or wind investments ahead of peak-period strain.

peakDemand.title: Peak Electricity Demand
peakDemand.subtitle: The highest amount of electricity needed at any single moment

explanation.what: This chart shows the highest recorded electricity demand per year across all Philippine grids.
explanation.why: Rising peak demand means the grid needs more reliable capacity. When peaks are too high, brownouts can happen.
explanation.action: Municipalities with high peak-demand growth should prioritize distributed solar or battery storage.

renewable.title: Clean Energy Generation
renewable.subtitle: How much electricity comes from solar, wind, hydro, and other clean sources

explanation.what: This chart shows total electricity generation from clean sources like solar, wind, hydro, and biomass each year.
explanation.why: A rising share means the country is successfully replacing coal and gas with cleaner energy. This helps reduce electricity costs and pollution over time.
explanation.action: You can explore solar, wind, or hydro options for your area if your province lags the national clean-energy growth trend.

explanation.what: This donut chart shows what share of the country's electricity comes from each source: coal, natural gas, oil-based, hydro, solar, wind, and biomass.
explanation.why: This helps you see how much of the country's electricity still comes from fossil fuels. A high fossil share usually means higher carbon emissions and prices that are affected by global fuel markets.
explanation.action: At home, you can reduce your own carbon footprint by using less electricity during peak hours or by considering rooftop solar where allowed.

glossary.solar_irradiance: The amount of sunlight reaching your area. More sunlight generally means more electricity can be produced by solar panels.
glossary.capacity_factor: Shows how efficiently a renewable energy system is expected to operate compared to its maximum possible output.
glossary.hydraulic_head: The height difference of flowing water. Greater height usually means more electricity can be generated.
glossary.payback_period: The estimated number of years needed to recover the cost of your renewable energy investment.
glossary.net_metering: A program where you can sell excess electricity back to the power company, reducing your bill even further.
glossary.kwh: Kilowatt-hour — the unit of electricity on your bill. One kWh is like running a 1,000-watt appliance for one hour.
glossary.mw: Megawatt — a large unit of power. One MW equals 1,000 kilowatts, enough to power hundreds of homes.
glossary.gwh: Gigawatt-hour — a very large amount of electricity, often used to measure national or regional energy use.
glossary.renewable_share: The percentage of electricity that comes from clean sources like solar, wind, hydro, or geothermal instead of fossil fuels.
glossary.fossil_fuels: Coal, oil, and natural gas. Burning them produces electricity but also releases pollution and carbon dioxide.
glossary.carbon_reduction: The amount of CO₂ (carbon dioxide) pollution you avoid by using clean energy instead of fossil fuels.
glossary.suitability_score: A rating from 0 to 100 that tells you how well a renewable energy type matches your location's conditions.
glossary.elevation: How high above sea level your location is. Higher areas can have different wind and temperature conditions.
glossary.transmission_charge: The cost of moving electricity from power plants to your area through large power lines.
glossary.distribution_charge: The cost of delivering electricity from local substations to your home through neighborhood power lines.
glossary.generation_charge: The cost of actually producing electricity at power plants. This is the biggest part of your electric bill.
glossary.utility_scale: Large power plants that serve thousands of homes, not something you can install in your backyard.
glossary.micro_hydro: A small water-powered generator for homes or small communities, using nearby streams or rivers.
glossary.rooftop_solar: Solar panels installed on your roof to generate electricity for your home.
glossary.off_grid: Being completely independent from the electric company by generating all your own power.
glossary.grid_tied: Connected to the electric company lines. You can use grid power when your solar or wind isn't producing enough.
glossary.inverter: A device that converts the electricity from solar panels into the type of electricity your home appliances use.
glossary.battery_storage: Batteries that store excess solar or wind energy for use at night or during cloudy days.
glossary.peak_demand: The highest amount of electricity the country needs at any single moment. High peaks can cause brownouts.
glossary.brownout: A temporary drop in electricity supply, causing lights to dim and appliances to work poorly.
glossary.blackout: A complete loss of electricity in an area, usually caused by storms or overloaded power systems.
glossary.municipality: A city or town with its own local government. We use this to match your area with local climate and resource data.
